scenes.tts: Can two lines that cross show that memory has more than one system? Watch one experiment.
scenes.visual: Title fades. Two lines on a blank chart slowly cross. The question appears.
scenes.narration: Can two lines that cross show that memory has more than one system? Watch one experiment.

scenes.tts: In 1996, Knowlton, Mangels and Squire gave people a weather prediction task.
scenes.caption: In 1996, Knowlton, Mangels and Squire gave people a weather-prediction task.
scenes.visual: Name card: Knowlton, Mangels and Squire, 1996. A screen shows cue cards and two outcome buttons.
scenes.narration: In 1996, Knowlton, Mangels and Squire gave people a weather-prediction task.

scenes.tts: Cue cards appeared, and the person guessed one of two outcomes. Each card predicted it only with some probability.
scenes.visual: Three cue cards light up, each with a small probability bar, none reaching the top. A cursor picks outcome 1 or 2; feedback flashes.
scenes.narration: Cue cards appeared, and the person guessed one of two outcomes. Each card predicted it only with some probability.

scenes.tts: No single trial is decisive, so the task is learned gradually, from feedback.
scenes.visual: Many trials stack up as thin strips; a learning line slowly rises through them.
scenes.narration: No single trial is decisive, so the task is learned gradually, from feedback.

scenes.tts: Afterwards, a questionnaire asked about the training sessions themselves.
scenes.visual: A questionnaire sheet with four answer boxes per question. Header: about the training. Corner label: illustrative design.
scenes.narration: Afterwards, a questionnaire asked about the training sessions themselves.

scenes.tts: Three groups took part: controls, amnesic patients, and patients with Parkinson's disease, whose striatum loses dopamine input.
scenes.visual: Three group icons: controls (grey), amnesic (blue), Parkinson's (orange). A small brain with the striatum highlighted and dopamine arrows thinning.
scenes.narration: Three groups took part: controls, amnesic patients, and patients with Parkinson's disease, whose striatum loses dopamine input.

scenes.tts: Over the first fifty trials, controls and amnesic patients learned the classification together. The Parkinson's patients failed to learn it.
scenes.visual: Left panel: percent correct against trials 1 to 50, dashed line at chance, 50%. Grey and blue curves rise together; orange stays low, near chance. Corner label: sketch of the pattern, not the published figure.
scenes.narration: Over the first fifty trials, controls and amnesic patients learned the classification together. The Parkinson's patients failed to learn it.

scenes.tts: Take the simplest difficulty model: one common capacity. Suppose the questionnaire is simply the harder task. The Parkinson's patients failed the easier one. How should they do on the questionnaire?
scenes.visual: Right panel appears with empty bars for the three groups. Label over the questionnaire: harder? Small tag at top: simple difficulty model, one common capacity. A question mark over the orange bar.
scenes.narration: Take the simplest difficulty model: one common capacity. Suppose the questionnaire is simply the harder task. The Parkinson's patients failed the easier one. How should they do on the questionnaire?

scenes.tts: On that model, they should fail it too. Instead, they remembered the training.
scenes.visual: The orange bar rises high.
scenes.narration: On that model, they should fail it too. Instead, they remembered the training.

scenes.tts: The amnesic patients had severely impaired memory for the training. Yet they learned the classification.
scenes.visual: The blue bar rises only a little and stays low. On the left panel, the blue curve glows where it rises with the grey one.
scenes.narration: The amnesic patients had severely impaired memory for the training. Yet they learned the classification.

scenes.tts: So no single order of difficulty fits both groups. Each group does far worse on the task the other does well, and the lines cross. These are group averages, so the crossing argues against the simplest difficulty account rather than ruling out every single-capacity one.
scenes.visual: The harder? label and the simple-difficulty-model tag fade. A two-task plot: classification left, questionnaire right. Blue and orange lines join each group's scores and cross in the middle. The crossing point pulses. Small caption under the plot: group averages; argues against one capacity, not proof.
scenes.narration: So no single order of difficulty fits both groups. Each group does far worse on the task the other does well, and the lines cross. These are group averages, so the crossing argues against the simplest difficulty account rather than ruling out every single-capacity one.

scenes.tts: Now, a trap. Some answers are right by guessing.
scenes.visual: A die rolls beside the bars. Label: guessing.
scenes.narration: Now, a trap. Some answers are right by guessing.

scenes.tts: In this illustrative design, guessing alone gets half right on the two choice task. On a four choice questionnaire, it gets a quarter.
scenes.caption: In this illustrative design, guessing alone gets half right on the two-choice task. On a four-choice questionnaire, it gets a quarter.
scenes.visual: Each panel gets a dashed baseline: 50% on classification, 25% on the questionnaire. Label: expected score from guessing. The plot area below each baseline stays visible.
scenes.narration: In this illustrative design, guessing alone gets half right on the two-choice task. On a four-choice questionnaire, it gets a quarter.

scenes.tts: So measure each score up from that baseline, as a share of the controls' gain above it.
scenes.visual: Formula on screen: relative score = (patient − chance) / (control − chance). An arrow measures from the baseline up to the bar top.
scenes.narration: So measure each score up from that baseline, as a share of the controls' gain above it.

scenes.tts: An invented bar that looks like half of normal shrinks to about a quarter.
scenes.visual: Invented numbers: patient 40%, controls 80%, chance 25%. The bar first reads 50% of normal, then is re-measured from the baseline and shrinks to 27%.
scenes.narration: An invented bar that looks like half of normal shrinks to about a quarter.

scenes.tts: The correction changes how big a loss looks. As long as controls beat chance, it cannot change which group is higher. So the crossing stays.
scenes.visual: Bars shrink and grow as each is re-measured from its baseline, but the blue and orange lines keep their order and still cross.
scenes.narration: The correction changes how big a loss looks. As long as controls beat chance, it cannot change which group is higher. So the crossing stays.

scenes.tts: Parkinson's disease damages more than the striatum. So this crossing supports separable learning processes, without pinning each to one structure.
scenes.visual: The striatum highlight spreads to faint other regions. Two process boxes stay, but their arrows to brain regions turn dashed. Small note: first 50 trials; see Going deeper.
scenes.narration: Parkinson's disease damages more than the striatum. So this crossing supports separable learning processes, without pinning each to one structure.

scenes.tts: Now a second crossing, in three patients.
scenes.visual: A grid: rows amygdala damage and hippocampal damage, columns sweat response and can report the pairing.
scenes.narration: Now a second crossing, in three patients.

scenes.tts: A signal was paired with an aversive stimulus. Did a sweat response appear? Could the patient report the pairing?
scenes.visual: A tone or coloured light is followed by an aversive stimulus icon. A skin-conductance trace rises; a speech bubble shows the paired signal.
scenes.narration: A signal was paired with an aversive stimulus. Did a sweat response appear? Could the patient report the pairing?

scenes.tts: A patient with damage to both amygdalae could report the pairing, but showed no conditioned response.
scenes.visual: Row 1 fills: sweat response, a cross; can report, a tick.
scenes.narration: A patient with damage to both amygdalae could report the pairing, but showed no conditioned response.

scenes.tts: A patient with damage to both hippocampi showed the reverse.
scenes.visual: Row 2 fills: sweat response, a tick; can report, a cross.
scenes.narration: A patient with damage to both hippocampi showed the reverse.

scenes.tts: Predict the third patient, with damage to both structures.
scenes.visual: A third row appears, labelled both, with question marks in both cells.
scenes.narration: Predict the third patient, with damage to both structures.

scenes.tts: That patient learned neither.
scenes.visual: Row 3 fills: two crosses.
scenes.narration: That patient learned neither.

scenes.tts: Two crossings. In these studies, new memory that could be reported and memory shown in performance depended on different structures.
scenes.visual: End card: Order shows the crossing. Chance shows the size.
scenes.narration: Two crossings. In these studies, new memory that could be reported and memory shown in performance depended on different structures.
